item.title: 3. Time sinks -- a game idea arises.
item.description:
🧱 Pixel Art: An Unexpected Obsession

I don’t really know how I got sucked into the world of Aseprite and pixel art so fast, but man — that rabbit hole is dangerous.

While fleshing out my ECS (Entity, Component, System) and rendering systems, I kept thinking: What will this game actually look like? How will it feel? Will it have a narrative? Will it be 2D or 3D?

It’s no secret that making a solo game is hard as hell — especially when you’re not using Blueprints or Unity’s editor. Once programming is under control, all that’s left is art and audio — which, funny enough, are exactly the areas where I have the least natural talent.

item.title: 1. Building a Game Engine - Why?
item.description:
What Do I Want to Code?

  1. Something that excites me and that I’m genuinely passionate about.
  2. Something that can be iterated and tinkered on for months or years.
  3. Something that strikes multiple domains, not just coding / learning code.
  4. Something that genuinely forces me to think technically.

After considering all of these, a game engine is just an obvious choice.

I’ve always been a gamer. I want to go back to my C++ roots, but in the most hardcore of ways.
I want to do something difficult.

item.title: 2. Mycelium Game Engine lives - What we've done so far.
item.description:
Gameplan

I needed a hook.

Why would I want to make a game on my engine? How is it different enough from Unreal or Unity to justify building a game on this, rather than one of those?

Truth is — it’ll never be fully justified. Those engines are simply too good. But I needed a hook regardless.

Entropy in Game Development as a first-class system

I could be off — way off. I’ve never done this before, and I have no idea what I’m doing. But I don’t think Unity or Unreal treat time — or rather, change over time — as a first-class system.
